questions.text: How many stars (*) will the following snippet send to the console?
questions.explanation: i goes 0->2 (print), 2->4 (print), then 4<=3 is False, loop ends. Two stars printed. Verified by running.

questions.text: How many stars (*) will the following snippet send to the console?
questions.explanation: i becomes 1 (odd, prints), then 2 (even, breaks before printing). Only one star printed. Verified by running.
questions.context:
i = 0
while i <= 5 :
    i += 1
    if i % 2 == 0:
        break
    print("*")

questions.text: How many hashes (#) will the following snippet send to the console?
questions.explanation: The for-loop runs once and prints one #. Since the loop completes without break, the else block also runs and prints another #. Total: two. Verified by running.
questions.context:
for i in range(1):
    print("#")
else:
    print("#")

questions.text: How many hashes (#) will the following snippet send to the console?
questions.explanation: var takes values 1,2,3,4,5,6; even values (2,4,6) hit continue and skip the print, so only odd values 1,3,5 print. Three hashes. Verified by running.
questions.context:
var = 0
while var < 6:
    var += 1
    if var % 2 == 0:
        continue
    print("#")

questions.explanation: var doubles each iteration via left shift: 1,2,4,8, then 16 stops the loop. Prints occur for var=1,2,4,8 -> four hashes. Verified by running.

questions.text: Take a look at the snippet, and choose the true statements: (Select two answers)
options: nums and vals are of the same length
nums is replicated and assigned to vals
nums and vals refer to the same list
questions.explanation: vals = nums assigns a reference, not a copy, so both names point to the same list object. Deleting a slice via vals affects the same list nums sees too, so both end up [1,3] with equal length. Verified by running.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences are true? (Select two answers)
options: nums and vals are of the same length
nums and vals are two different lists
questions.explanation: Slicing always creates a new list object, so vals is a distinct list from nums. The slice [-1:-2] is empty (invalid direction), so vals has length 0 while nums has length 3 -- nums is longer. Verified by running.

questions.text: What is the output of the following snippet?
questions.explanation: The list grows while being iterated by index, so my_list[v] keeps referencing shifted positions as elements get inserted at index 1. Actually running it step by step gives [1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3] -- this one is easy to get wrong by hand-tracing since the list mutates mid-loop.
questions.context:
my_list = [1, 2, 3]
for v in range(len(my_list)):
    my_list.insert(1, my_list[v])
print(my_list)

questions.text: What is the output of the following snippet?
questions.explanation: Every row of t is identical: [3, 2, 1] (since i is the inner loop variable regardless of j). Diagonal sum: t[0][0]+t[1][1]+t[2][2] = 3+2+1 = 6. Verified by running.
questions.context:
t = [[3-i for i in range(3)] for j in range(3)]
s = 0
for i in range(3):
    s += t[i][i]
print(s)
